target_year_over_year_context.explanation:
Both disclosures focus on the benefits of edge computing/device processing, specifically noting proximity to data, reduced response time, and improved privacy, security, and personalization.

Both disclosures describe mobile devices (handsets/PCs in 2024, mobile in 2023) becoming pervasive AI platforms where complex large generative AI algorithms run on-device to enable on-demand and contextual use cases.

Both disclosures outline the vision of generative AI becoming ubiquitous and expanding beyond smartphones into other industries such as IoT, XR, and automotive.

Both disclosures address the broader trend of generative AI capabilities in edge devices, with 2023 discussing the general vision of AI expansion and 2024 providing specific adoption forecasts for generative AI capable smartphones.

target_year_over_year_context.explanation:
The 2024 disclosures D008 and D009 jointly describe the trend of edge AI, focusing on context-aware processing benefits (privacy, security, personalization) and the emergence of mobile handsets/PCs as pervasive AI platforms with on-device generative AI. The 2025 disclosure D008 covers the same core trend, explicitly linking processor advancements to cloud/edge distribution, restating the benefits of edge computing (privacy, security, personalization), and describing smartphones/PCs as pervasive AI platforms with on-device generative AI. The 2025 text adds details about new personal AI devices (smart glasses, earbuds), but the primary subject of on-device AI trends and device platforms matches the combined 2024 input.

The 2024 disclosure envisions generative AI becoming ubiquitous, expanding into IoT, XR, and automotive. The 2025 disclosure (qcom_2025_1_D008) contains the nearly identical sentence: 'Building on the smartphone and PC foundation, we envision AI becoming ubiquitous... as it continues to expand into industries and applications such as industrial IoT, XR and automotive.' This is a direct topical match on the specific expansion vision.

comparisons.peer_topic: Hyperscale Customer Base and Product Applications
comparisons.peer_summary: AMD's data center products, including server CPUs, GPU accelerators, and adaptive SOCs, are purchased by large public cloud providers and hyperscale private data centers. These customers incorporate the products into servers for web applications, public cloud services, and AI workloads such as generative AI models.
comparisons.comparison: Both Qualcomm and AMD describe the expansion of AI workloads, specifically generative AI, into broader infrastructure and device markets. Qualcomm focuses on the ubiquity of generative AI across industries like IoT, XR, and automotive, driven by on-edge device capabilities. AMD highlights its role in supporting these AI workloads through data center products (GPU accelerators) purchased by hyperscale cloud providers and private data centers. While Qualcomm emphasizes the end-device expansion of generative AI, AMD emphasizes the underlying hardware infrastructure (data centers) that supports these workloads, including generative AI models.

sentences.text: Building on the smartphone and PC foundation, we envision generative AI becoming ubiquitous, continuing to expand into industries and applications such as IoT, XR and automotive.

Hyperscale data centers use these products to operate web-based applications or to support public cloud computing and storage service offerings, including but not limited to AI workloads such as generative AI models.

comparisons.peer_topic: Software strategy and open source contributions
comparisons.peer_summary: Intel aims to optimize AI frameworks and maintains the OpenVINO toolkit for deep learning inference. In 2024, Intel launched the Open Platform for Enterprise AI under the Linux Foundation and contributed oneAPI specifications to the UXL Foundation to enable open, multi-vendor programming across accelerators.
comparisons.comparison: Qualcomm and Intel both address the generative AI trend, but with different strategic focuses. Qualcomm envisions generative AI becoming ubiquitous across various industries and devices, emphasizing the expansion from smartphones and PCs. Intel focuses on the software and middleware stack required to optimize AI frameworks and accelerate inference for generative AI on its hardware. While Qualcomm describes the market expansion and application breadth of generative AI, Intel details the technical enablement via tools like OpenVINO and the Open Platform for Enterprise AI to run these workloads efficiently.

sentences.text: Building on the smartphone and PC foundation, we envision generative AI becoming ubiquitous, continuing to expand into industries and applications such as IoT, XR and automotive.

Our OpenVINO™ toolkit is an open source toolkit that accelerates deep learning inference on our processors across various use cases, such as generative AI, computer vision, audio, and language with industry standard models.
In 2024 we launched the Open Platform for Enterprise AI under the Linux Foundation to accelerate deployment of generative AI use cases through industry standard modular microservice architecture.

comparisons.peer_topic: PC market and AI-driven DRAM demand
comparisons.peer_summary: Next-generation PCs feature AI capabilities and high-performance neural processing chipsets, leading to significantly higher DRAM content, with the company announcing low-power compression-attached memory modules to support AI workloads on PCs.
comparisons.comparison: Qualcomm and Micron both identify the expansion of AI capabilities into next-generation Personal Computers (PCs) as a key market driver. Qualcomm notes that generative AI is expanding from its smartphone and PC foundation into broader industries. Micron specifies that next-generation PCs with AI capabilities and neural processing chipsets will have significantly more DRAM content, creating a specific demand driver for memory products. Both disclosures link the broader generative AI trend directly to the PC market evolution, though Qualcomm describes the platform shift while Micron describes the resulting component demand (DRAM).

sentences.text: Building on the smartphone and PC foundation, we envision generative AI becoming ubiquitous, continuing to expand into industries and applications such as IoT, XR and automotive.
The next generation PCs that have been announced contain high-performance neural processing chipsets as well as AI.
We expect these devices will have significantly more DRAM content than today's average PC.

comparisons.peer_summary: Gamers and creators choose NVIDIA GPUs for immersive experiences, with the market expanding due to live streamers and the advent of generative AI for local PC usage.
comparisons.comparison: Qualcomm and NVIDIA both discuss the expansion of generative AI into local PC usage. Qualcomm envisions generative AI becoming ubiquitous and expanding from smartphones and PCs into other industries. NVIDIA explicitly states that the advent of generative AI is driving PC users to choose GPUs for running generative AI applications locally on their PCs, citing privacy, latency, and cost benefits. Both disclosures highlight the shift towards local/on-device generative AI processing on personal computing devices.

sentences.text: Building on the smartphone and PC foundation, we envision generative AI becoming ubiquitous, continuing to expand into industries and applications such as IoT, XR and automotive.

With the advent of generative AI, we expect a broader set of PC users to choose NVIDIA GPUs for running generative AI applications locally on their PC, which is critical for privacy, latency, and cost-sensitive AI applications.
